name: TNY280GN-TL
title: TinySwitch-III TNY274-280: off-line ON/OFF switcher with 700 V MOSFET and selectable current limit
summary: The TNY274 to TNY280 put a 700 V power MOSFET and its controller in one 7-lead package (DIP-8C or SMD-8C, pin 3 absent) for flyback supplies run from rectified mains. Regulation is by ON/OFF cycle skipping at an average 132 kHz: each clock cycle runs or is skipped according to the EN/UV pin, so no loop compensation is needed. The chip powers itself from its DRAIN pin through a 0.1 µF BP/M capacitor, and the value of that capacitor (0.1, 1 or 10 µF) picks one of three current limits. Line undervoltage sensing, auto-restart, hysteretic thermal shutdown, output overvoltage latch-off and frequency jitter are built in. The seven sizes cover about 5 W to 36.5 W; the TNY280GN-TL is the largest, in SMD-8C on tape and reel.
key_figures: 132 kHz typ average, 8 kHz p-p jitter
750 mA typ (698 to 818 mA, G package)
14 W adapter, 28.5 W peak or open frame

notes: The name reads TNY, a three-digit series number (274 to 280), the package letter (G for SMD-8C, P for DIP-8C), the lead finish (N for RoHS compliant and halogen free; G, also RoHS compliant and halogen free, is not recommended for new designs) and an option (blank for the standard configuration, TL for tape and reel of 1000 pieces minimum and multiple, G package only).

A device's reduced current limit equals the standard limit of the next smaller device and its increased limit the standard limit of the next larger device; neighbouring devices can be exchanged with no other circuit change.

pins.name: EN/UV
pins.function: Enable and line undervoltage input. Pulling more than the threshold current (about -115 µA) out of the pin stops switching; switching resumes once the drawn current falls below it. A resistor from the DC bus to this pin sets the line undervoltage level; with no resistor present (under about 2 µA into the pin) the undervoltage function is off.

pins.name: BP/M
pins.function: Bypass and mode pin: the internal 5.85 V supply node, decoupled by an external capacitor to SOURCE. The capacitor value sets the current limit: 0.1 µF standard, 1 µF reduced (the next smaller device's standard limit), 10 µF increased (the next larger device's standard limit, TNY275-280). Current above ISD into the pin latches the device off until BP/M falls below 4.9 V; a Zener from a bias winding uses this for output overvoltage shutdown.

pins.name: D
pins.function: DRAIN: drain of the power MOSFET. The internal supply for start-up and running is drawn from this pin.

pins.name: S
pins.function: SOURCE: MOSFET source, return for the high-voltage current and common for the control circuits. Pins 5 to 8 are all SOURCE.

notes: Pin 3 is absent, which widens the creepage from DRAIN (pin 4) to the other pins. The SOURCE pins are tied to the lead frame and are the main path for heat.

circuits.title: TNY278P, 12 V, 1 A Universal Input Power Supply
circuits.description: Flyback converter from 85-265 VAC to an isolated 12 V at 1 A. F1 and varistor RV1 guard the input; bridge D1-D4 rectifies, and C1, L1 (in the negative leg) and C2 form a pi filter for differential-mode noise. The primary of T1 runs from the DC bus to DRAIN. D5 with VR1 plus R1 in parallel with R2-C4 clamps the leakage spike on DRAIN; R2 also limits reverse current in the slow glass-passivated D5, and R2-C4 damp transformer ringing. On the secondary, D7 rectifies into C10, and ferrite bead L2 with C11 filters the output. The output is held where it is just enough to conduct through VR3 (11 V) and the PC817A LED; the phototransistor then pulls current from EN/UV and skips cycles. R6 sets LED current and R4 bypasses the LED. A bias winding (pins 4-5) with R7, D6 and C6 feeds VR2 (28 V) and R3 into BP/M, latching the chip off if the loop opens (trip at about 17 V out). R8, optional, supplies BP/M from the bias winding so no-load input falls from 140 mW to 40 mW at 265 VAC. R5, optional, sets the line undervoltage start. C7 sets the current limit; C5 is the Y capacitor.

parts.note: optocoupler; A, K = LED, C, E = phototransistor
primary 1-3, bias 4-5, secondary 8-6; pin 2 and the end marked NC are not connected

Efficiency is above 80 %, no-load input below 50 mW at 265 VAC, and conducted EMI more than 12 dBµV under the EN55022 Class B limit.

operation.text: The clock runs continuously. At each rising clock edge the enable circuit is sampled: if EN/UV is not pulling more than the threshold current, the MOSFET turns on for that cycle; if it is, the cycle is skipped. A cycle once begun always finishes; it ends when drain current reaches the current limit or DCMAX ends. EN/UV sits at about 1.2 V from a source follower limited to 115 µA, which keeps the optocoupler quick. Output ripple is set by the output capacitor, the energy per cycle and the feedback delay.

From the pattern of enabled and skipped cycles the state machine judges the load. At heavy load it uses the highest current limit; at medium and light load it lowers the limit in steps, which pushes the effective switching frequency out of the audio band and lowers transformer flux density. Near full load nearly every cycle conducts; lighter loads skip more cycles and then use lower limits, down to a few cycles at very light load.

Average frequency is 132 kHz with about 8 kHz peak-to-peak jitter modulated at 1 kHz, to lower both average and quasi-peak EMI. The oscillator also gives the DCMAX signal. When the on time is under 400 ns at start-up or overload, the switching frequency is reduced to keep control of peak drain current.

operation.topic: Supply, 5.85 V regulator and 6.4 V clamp
operation.text: While the MOSFET is off, an internal regulator charges the BP/M capacitor to 5.85 V from the DRAIN voltage; while it is on, the chip runs from that capacitor. 0.1 µF is enough for decoupling and storage. If current is fed into BP/M through a resistor from a bias winding, a shunt clamps the pin at 6.4 V and the internal high-voltage source stops drawing from DRAIN, bringing no-load consumption well under 50 mW. At least 1 mA is the recommended bias feed.
In steady state the MOSFET stops if BP/M falls below 4.9 V and does not switch again until the pin has climbed back to 5.85 V.
Above a die temperature of about 142 °C the MOSFET is held off; it restarts when the die has cooled by about 75 °C. The wide hysteresis keeps a lasting fault from overheating the board.

operation.topic: Current limit and leading edge blanking
operation.text: When MOSFET current passes ILIMIT the switch turns off for the rest of the cycle. For tLEB after turn-on the comparator is blanked so that capacitive and rectifier recovery spikes do not end the pulse early. Current-limit operation gives good line ripple rejection and nearly constant power over input voltage.

An oscillator-clocked counter is reset each time EN/UV is pulled low. If EN/UV is not pulled low for 64 ms (overload, short circuit, open loop), switching stops for 2.5 s, then tries again, repeating until the fault is gone; in a short circuit this delivers under 3 % of maximum power. During line undervoltage the counter is halted, so the off period lasts until the line recovers.

Each cycle stays on until current limit is reached, even after DCMAX goes low, which lowers the minimum input voltage for regulation, lengthens hold-up and allows a smaller bulk capacitor. It is disabled during start-up until the output reaches regulation.

A resistor from the DC bus to EN/UV sets the start voltage: at power-up, or while auto-restart has switching off, more than 25 µA must flow into EN/UV before switching begins. Until then BP/M is held at 4.9 V; it rises to 5.85 V once the line is high enough. With 4 MΩ the threshold is 100 V. With the resistor fitted, at power-down the MOSFET switches for 64 ms after regulation is lost and then stays off without restarts while the line is low.
With 0.1 µF on BP/M the capacitor charges in about 0.6 ms; charge time scales with the capacitance chosen for the other current limits. The fast ON/OFF loop gives no output overshoot at turn-on.

0.1 µF on BP/M selects the standard limit, the usual choice for closed adapters. 1 µF selects the reduced limit, equal to the next smaller device's standard limit, lowering RMS currents and losses for thermally hard designs at the cost of peak power. 10 µF selects the increased limit, equal to the next larger device's standard limit, for higher peak or continuous power where heat allows. The TNY280's increased limit is 850 mA typ. The TNY274 has no increased limit. A device can be swapped for its neighbour with no other circuit change.

About 5.5 mA flowing into BP/M sets an internal latch that stops switching; the latch clears when BP/M drops below 4.9 V after the AC input is removed. The BP/M capacitor plus an internal filter keep noise from tripping it, so the capacitor sits close to BP/M and SOURCE. A bias winding of 15 V to 30 V works best, with the Zener about 6 V above it (28 V for a 22 V winding); a 10 Ω to 47 Ω resistor in series with the bias diode or the Zener adds filtering, and in series with the Zener also limits BP/M current.

Self-powered, no-load input is under 150 mW at 265 VAC. A bias winding feeding BP/M through a resistor brings it under 50 mW. The resistor is sized for the specified DRAIN supply current IS2: a first value gives 40 % more than its maximum to allow for bias voltage sag at light load, and its value is then raised for the lowest no-load power.

Cycle skipping can put audio-frequency energy into the transformer. Keeping peak flux density below 3000 Gauss (300 mT) and dip varnishing the transformer practically removes it; vacuum impregnation is not used because it raises primary capacitance and losses. Z5U ceramic capacitors in the clamp can also hum; a film or other dielectric cures it.
An RCD clamp, or a Zener of about 200 V with a diode across the primary, limits DRAIN voltage at turn-off. Keep the clamp's loop to the transformer and device short for EMI.

Ground at one point, from the input filter capacitor to the copper under the SOURCE pins. Put the BP/M capacitor right at the BP/M and SOURCE pins. Keep EN/UV traces short and clear of BYPASS, DRAIN and any node above source potential. Keep the loop of input capacitor, primary and device small. All four SOURCE pins go to a copper area under the device that is both ground and heat sink; it is a quiet node, so make it large. Connect the Y capacitor straight from the input filter capacitor's positive terminal to the secondary return; in a pi filter the inductor goes between the negative terminals of the two capacitors. Place the optocoupler close to the device and away from drain and clamp traces. Keep the secondary winding, output diode and output capacitor loop small, with more copper on the quiet cathode than the anode (a large anode area raises radiated EMI).

The no-resistor detection threshold on EN/UV is low (about 1 µA). Humidity together with contamination such as no-clean flux can let leakage above 1 µA reach EN/UV from nearby high-voltage pads such as BP/M and stop start-up. Designs with the undervoltage resistor fitted are unaffected. Where contamination is unknown, the supply is open frame or the pollution degree is high, and no UV resistor is used, a 390 kΩ resistor from EN/UV to SOURCE keeps leakage well below 1 µA. Normal surface insulation resistance with no-clean flux is well above 10 MΩ and gives no trouble.

VDS stays at or below 650 V at the highest input and peak overload power, leaving 50 V to the 700 V BVDSS. At the highest ambient, highest input and peak power, the drain current shows no transformer saturation and the leading-edge spike stays under ILIMIT(MIN) at the end of tLEB(MIN); drain current stays within the absolute maximum ratings. At full power, lowest input and highest ambient, the device, transformer, output diode and capacitors stay within their temperature limits; a SOURCE pin temperature of 110 °C maximum allows for RDS(ON) spread. A transient KP of 0.25 or more prevents IINIT being exceeded at turn-on.

Because the highest current limit and the frequency are fixed, delivered power is proportional to primary inductance times peak primary current squared. A design therefore sizes primary inductance for the maximum output; with a correctly chosen device, current reaches the limit before DCMAX.
